questions.prompt: You see this error in Swift 6: 'Call to main actor-isolated method in a synchronous nonisolated context'. How do you fix it?

options.explanation: discardableResult only silences unused return value warnings.

options.text: Convert the enclosing Swift class into an Objective-C category across all targets.
options.explanation: Objective-C categories do not solve Swift concurrency isolation.

options.text: Call the method with await from an async context or annotate the caller with @MainActor.
options.explanation: Adding await hops onto the main actor asynchronously, or marking the caller @MainActor isolates it.

options.text: Declare all parameter arguments using the pass-by-reference inout keyword modifier.
options.explanation: inout modifiers are for pass-by-reference mutation and do not fix isolation.

options.text: Because the Swift compiler forbids basic arithmetic operations outside struct declarations.

options.text: Because any concurrent task can write to unsynchronized global memory simultaneously, creating a data race.
options.explanation: Unsynchronized global variables allow simultaneous reads and writes across threads, causing data races.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended fix for a shared static variable that must be mutated by user interface code?

options.text: Wrap the variable in a lazy computed property returning an optional type.
options.explanation: Computed properties do not solve thread safety on shared mutable storage.

options.text: Cast the variable to AnyObject before passing it to background threads.
options.explanation: Casting to AnyObject retains reference semantics and does not synchronize access.

options.text: Declare the variable inside a C bridge header file using macro definitions.
options.explanation: Bridging through C headers does not provide Swift Concurrency safety.

options.text: It runs all framework methods on high priority background threads.

questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between Swift 5 and Swift 6 concurrency checking, and what does Swift 6 guarantee?

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift 5 had optional concurrency warnings while Swift 6 enables complete checking by default
Explains that concurrency warnings become hard compiler errors in Swift 6
States that compiling without errors in Swift 6 guarantees compile-time freedom from data races

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift 5, concurrency checking was optional and produced compiler warnings that could be ignored. Swift 6 enables complete strict concurrency checking by default, transforming data race warnings into hard compiler errors. Once code compiles cleanly in Swift 6, it is statically guaranteed to be free of data races.

questions.prompt: When migrating to Swift 6, you encounter the error 'Call to main actor-isolated method in a synchronous nonisolated context'. Describe two valid ways to resolve it.

rubric.criterion: Describes calling the method asynchronously with await from an async context
Describes annotating the calling function or class with @MainActor
Alternatively mentions MainActor.run or MainActor.assumeIsolated where appropriate

questions.modelAnswer: One way to resolve this error is by calling the method with `await` from an asynchronous context. This tells Swift to hop onto the main actor safely. A second way is to annotate the calling function or class with `@MainActor`. This isolates the caller so it executes directly on the main thread.

questions.prompt: Why are mutable global variables banned by default in Swift 6, and what are two safe ways to fix them?

rubric.criterion: Explains that mutable global variables allow concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes, creating data races
States converting to an immutable let constant if the value never changes
States isolating the variable to @MainActor or a custom actor

questions.modelAnswer: Mutable global variables allow any concurrent thread to read or write shared memory without synchronization. This produces data races. If the value never changes, you can fix it by changing `var` to an immutable `let` constant. If mutations are needed, you can isolate the variable with `@MainActor` or place it inside an actor.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the @preconcurrency attribute during Swift 6 migration, and when should you use it?

rubric.criterion: Explains that @preconcurrency suppresses or downgrades concurrency diagnostics for unannotated third-party dependencies
Explains that it is used during incremental migration when external libraries have not yet adopted Swift 6 annotations
Mentions that it should be removed once the dependency updates with native Sendable conformances

questions.modelAnswer: The `@preconcurrency` attribute suppresses strict concurrency errors caused by older third-party libraries that have not yet updated for Swift 6. You use it when importing external frameworks that lack `Sendable` annotations. It allows your project to compile in Swift 6 without waiting for external library updates.

questions.prompt: What does nonisolated(unsafe) do in Swift 6, and what risks does it introduce?

rubric.criterion: Explains that nonisolated(unsafe) opts a specific variable or property out of compiler isolation checks
States that it should only be used when thread safety is guaranteed manually with custom locks or queues
Warns that bugs in manual locking will still cause runtime data races because the compiler no longer checks it

questions.modelAnswer: `nonisolated(unsafe)` tells the Swift compiler to skip isolation checks on a specific variable or property. It is designed for legacy types where thread safety is managed manually using locks or dispatch queues. The risk is that it disables compiler verification. If the manual locking logic has bugs, runtime data races will occur without warning.
